questions.q: What does a Linux namespace do for a container?
options: It limits how much CPU and memory the container can consume
It gives a process an isolated view of one kind of system resource, like process IDs or the filesystem
It compresses the container's image to save disk space
It encrypts network traffic between containers
questions.explain: A namespace isolates what a process can see -- for example, the PID namespace means a container only sees its own processes.

questions.q: What problem do cgroups (control groups) solve?
options: They prevent two containers from being built from the same image
They limit and account for resources like CPU, memory, and I/O so one container can't starve others on the same host
They assign each container its own kernel
They give containers access to each other's filesystems
questions.explain: cgroups control what a group of processes can use -- without them, a single runaway container could consume all of a host's memory or CPU.

questions.q: In the technical sense, what is a Linux container?
options: A separate physical machine dedicated to one application
A virtual machine with a smaller guest operating system
One or more processes running with namespaces applied for isolation and cgroup limits applied for resource control
A compressed archive of an application's source code
questions.explain: Stripped to its kernel-level definition, a container is just processes running under namespaces (for isolation) and cgroups (for resource limits).

questions.q: When you run `ps aux` inside a running container, why do you only see that container's own processes?
options: Because the host firewall blocks visibility into other processes
Because the container is the only thing running on the physical machine
Because the PID namespace gives the container an isolated process-ID view starting from its own PID 1
Because Docker deletes the process list of every other container
questions.explain: The PID namespace isolates the process-ID space, so a container's view of running processes includes only its own, beginning at PID 1.

questions.q: At Northbridge Retail, what specifically stops a traffic spike in the catalog service from starving the checkout service of CPU on the same host?
options: Running checkout on a completely different physical data center
cgroup limits applied to each container, which cap and account for how much CPU it can consume
The PID namespace, which has nothing to do with CPU usage
Docker automatically pausing any container that receives high traffic
questions.explain: cgroups are the mechanism that limits and accounts for CPU (and memory, I/O) usage per container, preventing one container from starving others.
